That other Sarah was ladylike, I am sure, in her wildest moments, but there is something hurried and boisterous in this one's tricks that reminds me of some one who is making a merit of being jolly under depressing circumstances. The commencement of '61 promised much pleasure for the rest of the year, and though Secession was talked about, I do not believe any one anticipated the war that has been desolating our country ever since, with no prospect of terminating for some time to come. final_message:
A Quiet Day

It rained all morning, and so, for once, nobody came. No callers, no messengers, no one to tell us what the papers had left out. I confess I did not know what to do with myself. A whole day with nothing required of it! I stood in the hall a full minute, like a person who has been handed a parcel and cannot think where to put it.

Then I remembered the basket. It has sat by the window for three weeks, with Charlie's shirt on top, the sleeve still gaping where I tore it getting it off the fence. I sat down with it at last, and threaded my needle, and found that I was glad of it. There is a comfort in a small mending that can be finished. Everything else is so large and so unsettled; but a sleeve, a sleeve will close if you only pull the thread tight enough.

Mother has put me in charge of the pantry shelves, and I did them after dinner, though not with a good grace. I took everything down, wiped each shelf, and put everything back, and then, being dissatisfied, took it all down again. Now what does this prove? That I am a model housekeeper? Hardly. I think I wanted to have my hands busy and my head quiet, and the shelves obliged me twice over. There is something very mean in a jar of preserves that will not stand straight, and I told it so.

I will not pretend the quiet was entirely pleasant. Toward evening it grew heavy, and I caught myself listening for hoofbeats on the road, as I do every hour of every day. Nothing. Only the rain dripping from the eaves, and the clock, and Mother humming something under her breath that she does not know she is humming. I did not tell her. Let her have it.

So the sleeve is mended, and the shelves are straight, and the shirt is folded on the chair, waiting for a brother to wear it. That is the sum of the day. It seems very little to set down; and yet I find I do not want to let it go unrecorded. Some days are made of nothing but small things done well, and perhaps, if we are spared, we will look back and call them the best we had.

I am off to bed now. The needle goes back in its cushion, where I will know to find it.
